chapters.html:
About the exam (what is and is not verified)

Anthropic's official page names the credential "Claude Certified Architect – Foundations" and says it tests foundational knowledge across Claude Code, the Claude Agent SDK, the Claude API, and Model Context Protocol (MCP), validating that you can make informed decisions about trade-offs. Source: Anthropic Partner Academy exam page.
Not verified: the abbreviation "CCAR-F", the exact domains and weightings, question count, time limit, pass mark and eligibility. The official page does not state them in text, and I did not use unsourced third-party figures. Read the official exam guide PDF linked from that page and map it to the chapters below.

How this guide maps to the four named areas

Named areaCoverage here
Claude Agent SDK (primary focus)Chapters 2-12 in depth
Model Context ProtocolChapter 5, plus MCP in scenarios 4 and 6
Claude CodeCompared with the SDK (ch. 2); same engine, settings, permissions concepts
Claude APICompared with the SDK (ch. 2); structured outputs, tool-use loop

Core exam topic = squarely inside the four named areas. Supplementary = advanced/production topics that go beyond what the official page lists (chapters 10-11 and parts of 12).

Runnable code with a mock key and model

Every code sample is a real file in examples/. Each starts with a mock ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and a model id, and the output printed under it was captured by running that file against an offline mock of the SDK (mock/claude_agent_sdk), so no network or paid key is needed. The mock replays scripted model decisions; permissions, hooks, sessions, subagents and error subtypes mimic the documented SDK behaviour. Re-generate with python make_examples.py.

Every animation is also exported as a standalone animated GIF in the gifs/ folder (python make_gifs.py).

How to use it

  1. Read a chapter, press Play on each animation (nothing autoplays; Pause, Replay and Step buttons are independent per animation).
  2. Answer the chapter knowledge check before opening answers.
  3. Take the mock exam (chapter 15) in full-length mode.
Accuracy policy: API names were checked against the official Agent SDK docs on code.claude.com (November 2026). The SDK changes quickly: confirm signatures in the Python reference before relying on them. Code samples are illustrative, were not executed against a live API, and architectural patterns (e.g. approval queues) are design suggestions, not SDK features. All practice questions are original; none are real or leaked exam items.

chapters.title: Claude Agent SDK fundamentals
chapters.html:
Naming: the SDK was previously called the Claude Code SDK and was renamed the Claude Agent SDK. Python package: claude-agent-sdk (import claude_agent_sdk); TypeScript: @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk.

2.1 What the Agent SDK is

What is it?

The Claude Agent SDK is a library that lets your program run the same agent loop that powers Claude Code: Claude reasons, calls tools (read files, run commands, search the web, call your functions), looks at the results and repeats until the task is done. You write a prompt and options; the SDK runs the loop for you.

Why is it needed?

With the plain Anthropic API (the Messages API) you must write the loop: send messages, detect tool_use, run the tool, send back tool_result, manage context growth, handle permissions and retries. The Agent SDK gives you that harness (built-in tools, context management, permissions, hooks, MCP, sessions) ready-made.

How does it work?

Your app calls query() or ClaudeSDKClient. The SDK starts the agent runtime, which sends the conversation and tool definitions to Claude, executes returned tool calls (subject to permissions and hooks), appends results, and loops. The SDK streams typed messages back to you (SystemMessage, AssistantMessage, UserMessage carrying tool results, and finally ResultMessage).

Real-world analogy

The Messages API is a very smart consultant you must instruct step by step by letter. The Agent SDK is hiring that consultant into an office with a desk, files, a phone and a manager (permissions) - you just hand over the assignment.

Practical example

A compliance team wants an agent that scans a folder of contracts, extracts renewal dates and writes a CSV. With the SDK they enable Read/Glob/Grep/Write and give a prompt; no orchestration code is needed.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e01_query.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AssistantMessage, TextBlock, ToolUseBlock, ResultMessage

async def main():
    options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
        model=MODEL,
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Glob", "Grep"],   # pre-approved, read-only built-in tools
        max_turns=8,                              # safety cap on agent-loop iterations
        cwd="./contracts",                        # working directory for the tools
    )
    # query() returns an async iterator: nothing runs until we iterate
    async for msg in query(prompt="List every contract that renews in 2026.", options=options):
        if isinstance(msg, AssistantMessage):
            for block in msg.content:
                if isinstance(block, ToolUseBlock): print("[tool]", block.name, block.input)   # Claude chose a tool
                elif isinstance(block, TextBlock): print(block.text)                           # Claude's text
        elif isinstance(msg, ResultMessage):          # always the last message
            print(f"turns={msg.num_turns} cost=${msg.total_cost_usd} session={msg.session_id}")

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

[tool] Glob {'pattern': 'contracts/*.txt'}
[tool] Grep {'pattern': 'Renewal date: 2026', 'path': 'contracts/*.txt'}
Found 2 contracts renewing in 2026:
- acme.txt (2026-03-01)
- initech.txt (2026-09-30)
turns=2 cost=$0.0063 session=sess-0001

Reading the output

  • [tool] Glob: Step 1: Claude looked for contract files first.
  • [tool] Grep: Step 2: it searched inside them for 2026 renewals.
  • Found 2 contracts: The answer is built from the Grep result, not guessed.
  • turns=2: Two tool turns, a tiny cost estimate, and a session id for resume.

What happens at each step:

  1. ClaudeAgentOptions declares what the agent may do.
  2. query() starts the loop; nothing runs until you iterate.
  3. Claude calls Glob, then Read, then answers - each is a turn.
  4. ResultMessage carries final metrics and the session_id for later resume.

Architecture explanation

Your app → Agent SDK (typed API) → agent runtime (loop, context, tool dispatch) → Claude via the Anthropic API; tools, MCP servers and hooks hang off the runtime.

When to use it

Choose the SDK when the task needs multi-step tool use over files, code, the web or enterprise systems. Use the plain Messages API for single-shot generation, classification or when you want full control over every step.

Examination relevance

Know that the SDK owns the loop and ships built-in tools; the Messages API does not. Do not confuse SDK (library you embed) with the Claude Code CLI/app (an end-user product built on the same engine).

2.2 Agent execution loop and lifecycle

  1. Prompt enters (string or streamed input).
  2. Model call: Claude returns text and/or tool_use blocks.
  3. Gate: hooks → deny rules → permission mode / allow rules → can_use_tool.
  4. Tool execution and tool_result appended.
  5. Repeat until Claude responds without tool calls, max_turns is hit, or an error/interrupt occurs.
  6. ResultMessage with subtype (e.g. success or an error subtype), cost, usage, session id.

2.3 Comparisons that are commonly confused

AspectClaude Agent SDKClaude CodeAnthropic API (Messages)
DefinitionLibrary to embed the agent loop in your appReady-made coding assistant (CLI / desktop / IDE)Raw model endpoint
Who writes the loop?SDKProductYou
Built-in toolsYes (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob, WebSearch, WebFetch, Agent ...)Yes (same engine)No (you define tools; server tools such as web search are opt-in)
InterfacePython / TypeScript codeTerminal, IDE, desktopHTTP / client SDKs
Best forCustom agents in products, pipelines, servicesInteractive developer workChat, extraction, classification, custom orchestration
AspectAgent SDKTraditional function calling
LoopAutomaticManual: you detect tool_use, run, return tool_result
Tool setBuilt-ins + custom + MCPOnly what you implement
Permissions/hooksBuilt inWrite your own
Context/session mgmtBuilt in (resume, compaction)Your responsibility
ControlHigher-level, less granularMaximum granularity
Exam relevance: Typical scenario: "A team needs file-editing, shell and web tools with approvals in a few lines of code" → Agent SDK. "Simple structured extraction from one document" → Messages API.

2.4 Capabilities and limitations

  • Can: multi-step tool use, subagents, MCP, hooks, sessions, streaming, structured outputs, permission control.
  • Limits: bounded by context window and cost; non-deterministic; autonomous actions require governance; the runtime needs a host able to run its process (Node-based CLI is bundled/required depending on version); latency of multi-turn loops.

Knowledge check

Try each question first, then open the answer.

chapters.title: Agent configuration and execution
chapters.html:
3.1 ClaudeAgentOptions

What is it?

ClaudeAgentOptions is a dataclass bundling every runtime setting of an agent run: system prompt, model, tools, permission mode, MCP servers, subagents, hooks, session behavior, turn limits and working directory.

Why is it needed?

Configuration is how you shape what the agent knows, can do, and may do. Most architectural decisions in the exam map to one option.

How does it work?

You build the object once and pass it to query(options=...) or ClaudeSDKClient(options=...). The SDK forwards it to the runtime at startup.

Real-world analogy

A job description plus a badge: system prompt = the role, allowed_tools = the keys on the badge, permission_mode = how much supervision applies, max_turns = the time budget.

Practical example

A support-ticket triage agent: read-only tools, strict system prompt, max_turns=10, model set to a fast model, cwd pointing at the knowledge-base folder.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e02_options.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions
from show import show

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    system_prompt="You are a careful IT assistant.",   # role / behaviour
    model=MODEL,                        # which Claude model runs the loop
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep"],     # auto-approved tools (does NOT hide other tools)
    disallowed_tools=["Bash"],          # always blocked - deny beats allow
    permission_mode="default",          # default | acceptEdits | plan | dontAsk | bypassPermissions | auto
    max_turns=10,                       # cap on tool-use iterations
)

async def main():
    print("deny list:", options.disallowed_tools, "| mode:", options.permission_mode)
    async for msg in query(prompt="Please run the cleanup script.", options=options):
        show(msg)                       # Claude tries Bash -> the SDK refuses -> Claude explains

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

deny list: ['Bash'] | mode: default
[tool_use] Bash {'command': './cleanup.sh'}
[tool_result ERROR] Tool 'Bash' is in disallowed_tools
Bash is not permitted in this session, so I did not run the cleanup script.
-- success: turns=1 cost=$0.0042 session=sess-0001

Reading the output

  • deny list: Printed before the run to confirm the configuration we built.
  • [tool_use]: Claude still tried Bash: allow/deny lists do not change what Claude asks for.
  • [tool_result ERROR]: The SDK refused with "disallowed_tools": deny beats everything.
  • Bash is not permitted: Claude turned the refusal into a helpful answer. Turns=1 because only one tool was attempted.

What happens at each step:

  1. allowed_tools = pre-approval list; disallowed_tools = hard block that overrides allow.
  2. permission_mode sets the baseline for everything not explicitly listed.
  3. max_turns prevents runaway loops.

Architecture explanation

Options are the single configuration surface of the runtime layer in the SDK architecture diagram.

When to use it

Always. Create per-use-case option objects (research agent vs. editing agent) rather than one giant permissive configuration.

Examination relevance

Common trap: allowed_tools means "approve without asking", not "only these tools exist". To truly remove a tool use disallowed_tools (or restrict the tool set), and a deny rule always beats an allow.

3.2 System prompts and model selection

What is it?

The system prompt tells Claude its role and rules. You can pass a plain string, or the Claude Code preset with extra instructions appended. The model option picks the model.

Why is it needed?

Behavior, tone, output format and safety rules are controlled here. Different tasks need different cost/quality trade-offs (a small fast model for triage, a stronger one for analysis).

How does it work?

A string replaces the default prompt (so Claude loses built-in coding guidance); the preset form keeps Claude Code's tool-usage guidance and lets you append your own text. Filesystem settings (CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json) are controlled by setting_sources: per the migration guide, omitting it loads user, project and local settings, while setting_sources=[] isolates the run (verify against your installed version).

Real-world analogy

The system prompt is the employee handbook; the model is how senior the employee is.

Practical example

A finance agent appends "Never reveal account numbers; always show currency" to the preset prompt.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e03_prompt.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions
from show import show

# 1) Custom string: REPLACES the default prompt (narrow, non-coding agent)
custom = ClaudeAgentOptions(model=MODEL, allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep"],
                            system_prompt="Answer only from the provided HR policies.")
# 2) Preset + append: keeps Claude Code's built-in guidance and adds your rules
preset = ClaudeAgentOptions(model=MODEL, allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep"],
                            system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code",
                                           "append": "Always cite the policy file path."})
async def main():
    print("custom:", custom.system_prompt)
    print("preset:", preset.system_prompt)
    async for msg in query(prompt="Which policy covers remote work?", options=preset):
        show(msg)

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

custom: Answer only from the provided HR policies.
preset: {'type': 'preset', 'preset': 'claude_code', 'append': 'Always cite the policy file path.'}
[tool_use] Grep {'pattern': 'remote', 'path': 'hr/*.md'}
[tool_result] hr/remote.md:2:Employees may work remotely up to 3 days per week with manager approval.
[tool_use] Read {'file_path': 'hr/remote.md'}
[tool_result] # Remote work
Employees may work remotely up to 3 days per week with manager approval.
Per hr/remote.md: Employees may work remotely up to 3 days per week with manager approval.
-- success: turns=2 cost=$0.0063 session=sess-0001

Reading the output

  • custom:: A plain string replaces the default system prompt.
  • preset:: The preset form keeps Claude Code guidance and adds your append rule.
  • Per hr/remote.md: The appended rule worked: the answer cites the file path.
  • -- success: The final ResultMessage: subtype, number of tool turns, an estimated cost, and the session id you can resume later.

When to use it

Use a custom string for narrow, non-coding agents. Use the preset + append for agents that rely on file/shell tools.

Examination relevance

Know the difference between replacing and appending; know that model choice is an option, and subagents can override the model individually.

3.3 Query and execution patterns

PatternAPICharacteristicsUse when
One-shotquery(prompt=..., options=...)Async iterator; new session each call unless resumed; no interruptsBatch jobs, pipelines, single task
Interactive clientClaudeSDKClientLong-lived session; client.query() + receive_response(); supports interrupt(), hooks, can_use_tool, custom toolsChat UIs, multi-turn, approval flows
Streaming inputPass an AsyncIterable as promptLets you feed messages over timeRequired by can_use_tool with query()

3.4 Streaming, async execution and state

What is it?

Everything in the SDK is async: you consume an async iterator of messages as Claude works instead of waiting for one final blob.

Why is it needed?

Agent runs take seconds to minutes. Streaming lets you show progress, log tool calls live, and stop early.

How does it work?

async for msg in query(...) yields messages in order. With ClaudeSDKClient, await client.query(text) sends a turn and client.receive_response() yields messages until a ResultMessage. State = conversation history kept by the session (not Python variables).

Real-world analogy

Watching a live sports feed instead of reading tomorrow's newspaper.

Practical example

A chat UI that prints "Reading policy.pdf…" as soon as a ToolUseBlock appears.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e04_client.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeSDKClient, ClaudeAgentOptions
from show import show

async def main():
    opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(model=MODEL, allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep"])
    async with ClaudeSDKClient(options=opts) as client:       # one persistent session
        await client.query("What does our PTO policy say?")   # turn 1
        async for msg in client.receive_response():           # stream until this turn's ResultMessage
            show(msg)
        print("----- turn 2 (same session) -----")
        await client.query("And for contractors?")            # turn 2 relies on turn 1 context
        async for msg in client.receive_response():
            show(msg)

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

[tool_use] Grep {'pattern': 'PTO', 'path': 'hr/*.md'}
[tool_result] hr/contractors.md:2:Contractors do not accrue PTO; time off is agreed in the statement of work.
hr/pto.md:1:# PTO Policy
hr/pto.md:2:Employees accrue 20 days of PTO per year.
[tool_use] Read {'file_path': 'hr/pto.md'}
[tool_result] # PTO Policy
Employees accrue 20 days of PTO per year.
Up to 5 unused days carry over.
Employees accrue 20 days of PTO per year; 5 unused days carry over.
-- success: turns=2 cost=$0.0063 session=sess-0001
----- turn 2 (same session) -----
[tool_use] Read {'file_path': 'hr/contractors.md'}
[tool_result] # Contractors
Contractors do not accrue PTO; time off is agreed in the statement of work.
(following up on: What does our PTO policy say?)
Contractors do not accrue PTO; time off is set in the statement of work.
-- success: turns=1 cost=$0.0042 session=sess-0001

Reading the output

  • [tool_use] Grep: Turn 1: find the policy.
  • ----- turn 2: A second client.query() in the same session.
  • (following up on:: Proof of memory: Claude knew "contractors" referred to the PTO question without being told.
  • session=sess-0001: Both turns share one session id.

Architecture explanation

Streaming sits between the runtime and your app: typed messages are the contract for progress, tool visibility and final results.

When to use it

query() for fire-and-forget; ClaudeSDKClient when you need continuity, interrupts or interactivity.

Examination relevance

Client vs query: client = same session across turns, supports interrupt; query = single exchange. Message order always ends with a ResultMessage.

Knowledge check

Try each question first, then open the answer.

flow.title: Tool lifecycle: Claude asks, your @tool answers

chapters.title: Built-in and custom tools
chapters.html:
4.1 Built-in tools and the tool lifecycle

What is it?

Tools are actions Claude can request. The SDK ships built-in tools so the agent can work with files, the shell and the web without you writing code.

Why is it needed?

An LLM alone can only produce text. Tools give it hands: read data, change files, run commands, fetch pages.

How does it work?

Claude emits a ToolUseBlock (name + JSON input). The SDK runs hooks and permission checks, executes the tool, and returns a ToolResultBlock (is_error flags failures; Claude sees the error and can retry or change approach).

Real-world analogy

A workshop: Claude is the craftsperson asking an assistant to fetch or operate a specific instrument; a supervisor (permissions) may say no.

Practical example

Code-fix agent: Grep finds the failing function, Read opens the file, Edit patches it, Bash runs the tests.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e05_tools.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AssistantMessage, ToolUseBlock

opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(model=MODEL, allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"])   # read-only agent

async def main():
    async for m in query(prompt="Where is retry logic implemented?", options=opts):
        if isinstance(m, AssistantMessage):
            for b in m.content:
                if isinstance(b, ToolUseBlock):
                    print("tool_use ->", b.name, b.input)       # observe every invocation

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

tool_use -> Grep {'pattern': 'retry', 'path': 'logs/*.log'}
tool_use -> Read {'file_path': 'logs/web.log'}

Reading the output

  • tool_use -> Grep: Claude searched first (cheap, narrow).
  • tool_use -> Read: Then opened the one relevant file. Searching before reading keeps context small.

Architecture explanation

Tool runtime sits after the gate (hooks → permissions) and returns results into the loop (see Tool execution architecture).

When to use it

Prefer built-ins when they fit; add custom tools only for domain-specific actions.

Examination relevance

Tool failures are returned to Claude as results (not exceptions in your app); Claude decides whether to retry.

ToolPurposeRisk / note
ReadRead a file (text, images, PDFs)Low; read-only
WriteCreate/overwrite a fileModifies files; gated by permissions
EditExact string replacement in a fileModifies files; fails if match not unique
BashRun shell commandsHighest risk: arbitrary command execution; restrict/sandbox
GrepRegex content searchRead-only. Docs say Grep/Glob may be absent by default on some platforms - verify in your environment
GlobFile-name pattern searchRead-only (same availability note)
AgentLaunch a subagent (named Task in older versions; the init tools list may still show "Task")Must be in allowed_tools for delegation; match both names when parsing
WebSearchSearch the webUntrusted results → prompt-injection surface
WebFetchFetch and read a URLSame; consider domain restrictions
Verified against code.claude.com tools-reference and agent-loop pages (Nov 2026). Other built-ins exist (NotebookEdit, Skill, AskUserQuestion, task tools replacing legacy TodoWrite, etc.) - the list evolves, so consult the official tools reference.

4.2 Custom tools with @tool

What is it?

A custom tool is your own Python function exposed to Claude. You decorate it with @tool(name, description, input_schema) and bundle it with create_sdk_mcp_server.

Why is it needed?

Built-in tools cannot know your business systems (inventory, CRM, pricing). Custom tools expose them safely with typed inputs.

How does it work?

The handler is async def f(args: dict) -> dict returning {"content": [{"type":"text","text":...}], "is_error": bool}. The tool runs in your process. Names become mcp__<server>__<tool>; add them to allowed_tools to pre-approve.

Real-world analogy

Adding a new button to the assistant's phone: a clearly labeled, typed action.

Practical example

Inventory agent that checks stock before quoting delivery dates.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e06_custom.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import tool, create_sdk_mcp_server, ClaudeAgentOptions, query
from show import show

@tool("check_stock", "Return units in stock for a SKU", {"sku": str})   # name, description (Claude reads it), schema
async def check_stock(args):
    stock = {"A-100": 42, "B-200": 0}                    # stand-in for a database call
    n = stock.get(args["sku"])
    if n is None:
        return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Unknown SKU"}], "is_error": True}   # error goes back to Claude
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"{args['sku']}: {n} in stock"}]}

server = create_sdk_mcp_server(name="inventory", version="1.0.0", tools=[check_stock])

opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    model=MODEL,
    mcp_servers={"inventory": server},                   # register under the key "inventory"
    allowed_tools=["mcp__inventory__check_stock"],       # mcp__<server>__<tool>
)
async def main():
    for prompt in ["Do we have SKU A-100?", "Do we have SKU Z-999?"]:
        print(">>", prompt)
        async for m in query(prompt=prompt, options=opts):
            show(m)

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

>> Do we have SKU A-100?
[tool_use] mcp__inventory__check_stock {'sku': 'A-100'}
[tool_result] A-100: 42 in stock
A-100 has 42 in stock.
-- success: turns=1 cost=$0.0042 session=sess-0001
>> Do we have SKU Z-999?
[tool_use] mcp__inventory__check_stock {'sku': 'Z-999'}
[tool_result ERROR] Unknown SKU
SKU Z-999 is not in the catalogue, so I cannot quote stock.
-- success: turns=1 cost=$0.0042 session=sess-0002

Reading the output

  • >> Do we have SKU A-100?: Prompt 1: a SKU that exists.
  • mcp__inventory__check_stock: Custom tool name format: mcp__<server>__<tool>.
  • A-100: 42 in stock: Whatever your function returns becomes the tool result.
  • [tool_result ERROR]: Prompt 2: your function returned is_error, which Claude saw.
  • not in the catalogue: Claude explained the problem instead of inventing a number.

Architecture explanation

In-process MCP server: no subprocess or network hop, so your function can use local state and credentials.

When to use it

Use for private business logic. Use an external MCP server when the tool is shared across apps/languages or already exists.

Examination relevance

Remember the mcp__server__tool naming and that is_error reports failure to Claude. Tool descriptions are prompts: vague descriptions cause wrong tool selection.

4.3 Tool restrictions and orchestration

  • Restrict: disallowed_tools, narrow allowed_tools, hooks, permission modes, subagent tools lists.
  • Orchestrate: Claude may call several tools in one turn; read-only tools (annotated readOnlyHint) can run in parallel. Chain dependencies naturally by results.
  • Annotations: ToolAnnotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) describe behavior.
  • MCP wildcards: allowed_tools=["mcp__github__*"] is valid; a global * is ignored.

chapters.title: MCP architecture and integration
chapters.html:
5.1 Model Context Protocol (MCP)

What is it?

MCP is an open protocol that standardizes how AI applications connect to tools, data (resources) and reusable prompts. The AI app hosts an MCP client; each integration is an MCP server.

Why is it needed?

Without a standard, every tool×app pair needs custom glue. With MCP, write a server once and any MCP client (Claude Code, Agent SDK, others) can use it.

How does it work?

Client and server exchange JSON-RPC messages over a transport: stdio (local subprocess), http (remote streamable HTTP) or sse (legacy remote). The client calls tools/list then tools/call. Servers expose three primitives: tools (actions), resources (data), prompts (templates).

Real-world analogy

USB-C for AI: one port shape, many devices.

Practical example

An enterprise assistant connects to a GitHub MCP server (HTTP) and a local filesystem server (stdio).

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e07_mcp.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, SystemMessage
from show import show

opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    model=MODEL,
    mcp_servers={
        "fs":  {"command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/data"]},   # stdio transport
        "crm": {"type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.example.com/crm",                                    # remote HTTP transport
                "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer ${CRM_TOKEN}"}},
    },
    allowed_tools=["mcp__fs__*", "mcp__crm__lookup_customer"],   # wildcard per server; names are mcp__<server>__<tool>
)
async def main():
    async for m in query(prompt="Look up customer C-77 in the CRM", options=opts):
        if isinstance(m, SystemMessage):
            print("connected servers:", m.data["mcp_servers"])
            print("mcp tools:", [t for t in m.data["tools"] if t.startswith("mcp__")])
        else:
            show(m)

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

connected servers: [{'name': 'fs', 'status': 'connected'}, {'name': 'crm', 'status': 'connected'}]
mcp tools: ['mcp__fs__read_file', 'mcp__crm__lookup_customer']
[tool_use] mcp__crm__lookup_customer {'id': 'C-77'}
[tool_result] {"id": "C-77", "name": "Globex", "tier": "gold"}
Customer C-77 is Globex (tier: gold).
-- success: turns=1 cost=$0.0042 session=sess-0001

Reading the output

  • connected servers: The init message lists every MCP server that connected.
  • mcp tools: Discovered tool names, ready to be allowed or denied.
  • lookup_customer: Claude called the CRM tool over the MCP client.
  • "tier": "gold": External system data returned as a tool result; Claude summarised it.

Architecture explanation

Agent → built-in MCP client → transport → MCP server → external system; results return the same way.

When to use it

Use MCP for integrations shared across apps or maintained by others. Use SDK tools for app-private logic.

Examination relevance

Know client vs server roles, the three primitives, transports, and the tool-name format.

5.2 SDK-created MCP servers

What is it?

create_sdk_mcp_server(name, version, tools) builds an in-process MCP server from @tool functions (type "sdk").

Why is it needed?

Avoids running separate processes, handling IPC and deployment of another service for simple custom tools.

How does it work?

The returned config goes into mcp_servers. The SDK routes tool calls to your Python functions directly.

Real-world analogy

A built-in extension vs. a separately installed app.

Practical example

See chapter 4.2 inventory server.

When to use it

Single-app tools needing local state. Choose standalone when multiple clients/languages need it, or it must be isolated/sandboxed separately.

Examination relevance

In-process = no network/subprocess, same security boundary as your app.

5.3 Authentication, authorization and security

  • Auth: pass tokens via headers/env from a secret store; never hard-code. Server-side, authorize per user (OAuth scopes), not just per agent.
  • Least privilege: expose narrow tools (get_invoice) rather than raw SQL; allow only needed tools.
  • Untrusted servers: third-party MCP servers run code or return text that may contain prompt injection; vet, pin versions, log calls.
  • Human approval for write/destructive tools.

chapters.title: Subagents and multi-agent systems
chapters.html:
6.1 Subagents and the Agent tool

What is it?

A subagent is a specialized agent the main agent can delegate to through the Agent tool. It has its own prompt, tools and (optionally) model, and runs in an isolated context.

Why is it needed?

Keeps the main context clean (only a summary comes back), allows specialization and least-privilege tools, and enables parallel work.

How does it work?

Define subagents in agents={"name": AgentDefinition(description, prompt, tools, model)} and include "Agent" in allowed_tools. Claude picks a subagent from its description (or you name it). The subagent runs, and its final message returns to the parent as the tool result. Subagents cannot see the parent history, so the delegation prompt must carry needed context.

Real-world analogy

A manager hands a self-contained brief to a specialist and only reads the specialist's memo, not their whole notebook.

Practical example

A due-diligence agent delegates "find risks in contracts" to a read-only reviewer and "compute exposure" to an analyst with Bash.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e08_sub.py (mock API key + model included).

import os, asyncio

MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AgentDefinition
from show import show

opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    model=MODEL,
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob", "Agent"],       # "Agent" enables delegation (older docs call it "Task")
    agents={
        "researcher": AgentDefinition(
            description="Finds and summarizes relevant facts in the docs folder.",   # how Claude decides to delegate
            prompt="You are a meticulous researcher. Return bullet findings with file names.",
            tools=["Read", "Grep", "Glob"],                # least privilege
            model="haiku",                                 # cheaper model for retrieval
        ),
        "analyst": AgentDefinition(
            description="Analyzes findings and quantifies risk.",
            prompt="You analyze provided findings and produce a risk table.",
            tools=["Read"],
            model="sonnet",
        ),
    },
)
async def main():
    async for m in query(prompt="Use researcher then analyst to assess renewal risk in ./contracts", options=opts):
        show(m)       # indented lines = messages produced inside a subagent's own context

asyncio.run(main())

chapters.title: Hooks and lifecycle management
chapters.html:
7.1 Hooks

What is it?

Hooks are callbacks that the SDK runs at defined points in the agent lifecycle. You register them in ClaudeAgentOptions(hooks={...}) using HookMatcher.

Why is it needed?

Prompts are suggestions; hooks are deterministic enforcement. Use them to block dangerous calls, rewrite inputs, log, audit, inject context or notify.

How does it work?

At an event the SDK finds matchers whose regex matcher matches the tool name (None = all) and awaits each callback async def cb(input_data, tool_use_id, context). Return {} to proceed, or a hookSpecificOutput with permissionDecision ("allow", "deny", "ask", "defer") and a reason. If several PreToolUse hooks disagree: deny beats defer beats ask beats allow.

Real-world analogy

Security checkpoints and CCTV along a corridor: they inspect everyone passing, independent of what the traveler intends.

Practical example

Block any Bash command containing rm -rf, and log every tool result to an audit file.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e09_hooks.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, HookMatcher
from show import show

async def block_dangerous(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    cmd = input_data["tool_input"].get("command", "")
    if "rm -rf" in cmd:
        return {"hookSpecificOutput": {
            "hookEventName": "PreToolUse",
            "permissionDecision": "deny",                       # stop the tool before it runs
            "permissionDecisionReason": "Destructive command blocked by policy"}}
    return {}                                                   # empty dict = no objection

async def audit(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    print("   AUDIT:", input_data["tool_name"], "->", str(input_data["tool_response"])[:40])
    return {}

opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    model=MODEL,
    allowed_tools=["Bash"],
    hooks={
        "PreToolUse":  [HookMatcher(matcher="Bash", hooks=[block_dangerous])],
        "PostToolUse": [HookMatcher(hooks=[audit])],            # no matcher = every tool
    },
)
async def main():
    async for m in query(prompt="Clean the build folder", options=opts):
        show(m)

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

[tool_use] Bash {'command': 'rm -rf build/'}
[tool_result ERROR] Blocked by hook: Destructive command blocked by policy
[tool_use] Bash {'command': 'ls build/'}
   AUDIT: Bash -> app.bin  main.o
[tool_result] app.bin  main.o
Build folder inspected safely: app.bin  main.o
-- success: turns=2 cost=$0.0063 session=sess-0001

Reading the output

  • [tool_use]: Claude first tried to delete the build folder.
  • [tool_result ERROR]: The PreToolUse hook returned deny, so the command never ran. Claude was told why.
  • AUDIT:: The PostToolUse hook only fires for calls that actually ran.
  • Build folder inspected safely: Claude chose a safe alternative after the block.

Architecture explanation

Hooks wrap the tool gate (see Hook execution architecture): PreToolUse before permissions, PostToolUse after execution.

When to use it

Hooks for enforcement/observability that must always happen. Tools are things Claude chooses to call; hooks run whether or not Claude wants them.

Examination relevance

Python hook events (verified): PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, Notification, SubagentStart, PermissionRequest. TypeScript supports more (e.g. SessionStart/SessionEnd as callbacks) - in Python those work only as shell-command hooks from settings files. A hook "allow" does not bypass deny rules.

chapters.title: Sessions and context management
chapters.html:
8.1 Sessions, resume and fork

What is it?

A session is the persisted conversation (messages, tool calls, results) identified by a session_id. Context is what is inside the model's window right now. Sessions are storage; context is working memory.

Why is it needed?

Long tasks span many turns or processes. Sessions let you pause, resume, and branch without re-explaining.

How does it work?

The init SystemMessage (and the final ResultMessage) carry the session id. Pass resume=session_id to continue; add fork_session=True to branch into a new id leaving the original untouched; continue_conversation=True resumes the most recent session in the cwd. ClaudeSDKClient keeps its session across query() calls. Transcripts are stored as JSONL under ~/.claude/projects/ by default.

Real-world analogy

A saved game file (session) versus what is on your screen (context). Forking = save-as a new file.

Practical example

An analyst reviews a report overnight; next morning the agent resumes, then forks to explore an alternative conclusion.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e10_session.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage, AssistantMessage, TextBlock

async def run(prompt, **kw):
    sid, text = None, ""
    async for m in query(prompt=prompt, options=ClaudeAgentOptions(model=MODEL, allowed_tools=["Read"], **kw)):
        if isinstance(m, AssistantMessage):
            text = "".join(b.text for b in m.content if isinstance(b, TextBlock)) or text
        if isinstance(m, ResultMessage):
            sid = m.session_id                          # capture for later resume
    return sid, text

async def main():
    sid, t = await run("Read report.md and remember the key numbers.");      print("1)", sid, t)
    _, t = await run("What was the revenue figure?", resume=sid);              print("2) resumed:", t)
    _, t = await run("What was the revenue figure?");                          print("3) fresh session:", t)
    branch, t = await run("Assume revenue is 10% lower; redo the summary.",
                          resume=sid, fork_session=True)                       # new id, original untouched
    print("4) fork:", branch, "!=", sid, "->", t)

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

1) sess-0001 Noted: revenue is $4.2M and growth is 12%.
2) resumed: Revenue was $4.2M (recalled from earlier in this session).
3) fresh session: I have no earlier context about a revenue figure.
4) fork: sess-0003 != sess-0001 -> Branch summary: revenue falls to $3.78M (-10%) with growth under review.

Reading the output

  • 1) sess-0001: Call 1 starts a new session; we capture its id.
  • 2) resumed: resume=sid reloaded the history, so Claude remembered the revenue figure.
  • 3) fresh session: No resume, no memory: a brand-new session.
  • 4) fork: Forking created a new session id (sess-0003) with the old history; the original stays unchanged.

Architecture explanation

Session store (transcript files or a custom session_store) sits beside the runtime; resume loads history into a new context.

When to use it

Resume for continuity; fork for what-if exploration; new session for unrelated tasks (avoids polluted context).

Examination relevance

Forking branches conversation, not files (use file checkpointing for file rollback). Do not sum total_cost_usd across resumed results of the same session.

8.2 Context window, compaction and tokens

  • Every turn re-sends history, so cost and latency grow with conversation length; tool outputs (big files, command logs) are the usual culprits.
  • When context nears the limit the runtime compacts (summarizes) earlier history; a PreCompact hook lets you react. Persistent rules should live in the system prompt/CLAUDE.md, which are re-injected.
  • Strategies: subagents for noisy work, targeted Grep before Read, short tool outputs, split work across sessions, get_context_usage() on the client to inspect usage.
  • Memory beyond the window = files (notes, CLAUDE.md) or external stores the agent reads.

chapters.title: Security, permissions and governance
chapters.html:
9.1 Permission modes, rules and callbacks

What is it?

Permissions decide whether a tool call may run. Layers: hooks → deny rules → ask rules → permission mode → allow rules → can_use_tool callback.

Why is it needed?

Agents act autonomously; without guardrails one bad prompt or injected instruction could delete data or leak secrets.

How does it work?

Modes: default (unmatched calls go to your callback), acceptEdits (auto-approve file edits inside the working directory), plan (no execution; planning), dontAsk (deny anything not pre-approved), bypassPermissions (approve everything not denied - use only in isolated sandboxes), auto (classifier-based). Deny rules apply even in bypass mode. can_use_tool returns PermissionResultAllow or PermissionResultDeny(message=...); with query() it needs streaming input and a keep-alive hook (see docs).

Real-world analogy

Building access: always-denied rooms (deny), keycard doors (allow), and "ask the receptionist" (callback).

Practical example

A DevOps agent may read logs freely but must obtain human approval before restarting a service.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e11_perm.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import ClaudeSDKClient, ClaudeAgentOptions, PermissionResultAllow, PermissionResultDeny
from show import show

HUMAN_SAYS = {"answer": "no"}          # stands in for a real person clicking Approve/Deny

async def can_use_tool(tool_name, tool_input, context):
    if tool_name == "Bash" and "restart" in tool_input.get("command", ""):
        print(f"   [approval requested] {tool_input['command']!r} -> human says {HUMAN_SAYS['answer']!r}")
        if HUMAN_SAYS["answer"] == "yes":
            return PermissionResultAllow()
        return PermissionResultDeny(message="Operator declined the restart")
    return PermissionResultAllow()

opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    model=MODEL,
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Grep"],     # auto-approved (never reach the callback)
    disallowed_tools=["WebFetch"],      # hard deny
    can_use_tool=can_use_tool,          # decides everything else
)
async def main():
    for answer in ["no", "yes"]:
        HUMAN_SAYS["answer"] = answer
        print(f"=== run with human answer: {answer} ===")
        async with ClaudeSDKClient(options=opts) as client:
            await client.query("Restart the web service and check its logs")
            async for m in client.receive_response():
                show(m)

asyncio.run(main())

Reading the output

  • === run with human answer: no: Run 1: the reviewer declines.
  • [approval requested]: Only the restart reached the callback; reads were pre-approved.
  • [tool_result ERROR]: Deny message returned to Claude.
  • === run with human answer: yes: Run 2: same agent, approved this time.
  • web.service restarted: The tool actually ran only after approval.

Architecture explanation

Defense in depth: policy (hooks/rules) + approval (callback) + isolation (sandbox, container, least-privilege credentials).

When to use it

Use modes/rules for static policy; callbacks for dynamic or human decisions.

Examination relevance

Permission modes = coarse baseline; callbacks = per-call logic. allowed_tools does not restrict bypassPermissions. Deny always wins.

9.2 Prompt injection, sandboxing and governance

  • Prompt injection: text from web pages, files or MCP results may contain instructions. Treat tool output as data; limit tools after reading untrusted content; require approval for side effects; never give one agent both untrusted input and powerful credentials.
  • Sandboxing: run in containers/VMs, scope cwd/add_dirs, restrict network, mount read-only, use the sandbox option where supported; never run bypassPermissions on a developer's real machine.
  • Governance: central policy via settings, hooks for audit logs (who/what/when), cost caps (max_budget_usd), versioned prompts, review of MCP servers.

chapters.title: Advanced Agent SDK concepts
chapters.html:
10.1 Structured outputs

What is it?

Ask the agent to return JSON that conforms to a JSON Schema via output_format.

Why is it needed?

Downstream code needs machine-readable results, not prose.

How does it work?

output_format={"type": "json_schema", "schema": ...}; the validated object appears in ResultMessage.structured_output. If validation keeps failing the result subtype is error_max_structured_output_retries. With Pydantic use Model.model_json_schema().

Real-world analogy

A form with fixed fields instead of a free-text letter.

Practical example

Extract {vendor, amount, due_date} from invoices into a database.

Code implementation

Runnable file examples/e12_struct.py (mock API key + model included).

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage

schema = {"type": "object",
          "properties": {"vendor": {"type": "string"}, "amount": {"type": "number"}, "due_date": {"type": "string"}},
          "required": ["vendor", "amount", "due_date"]}

opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(model=MODEL, allowed_tools=["Read"],
                          output_format={"type": "json_schema", "schema": schema})

async def main():
    async for m in query(prompt="Extract fields from invoice.txt", options=opts):
        if isinstance(m, ResultMessage) and m.subtype == "success":
            data = m.structured_output                      # already validated against the schema
            print("structured_output:", data)
            print("amount + 10% tax =", round(data["amount"] * 1.10, 2))   # usable typed data, no text parsing

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured by actually running this file against the offline mock SDK):

structured_output: {'vendor': 'Acme', 'amount': 1250.0, 'due_date': '2026-12-01'}
amount + 10% tax = 1375.0

Reading the output

  • structured_output:: A validated Python dict, shaped by the schema.
  • amount + 10% tax: Because the data is typed, normal arithmetic just works.

When to use it

Whenever another program consumes the answer.

Examination relevance

Know the option name, the result field, and the failure subtype.

10.2 Errors, retries, cost, monitoring

Runnable file examples/e13_errors.py

Show full code (copy) and captured output
import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, ResultMessage, ClaudeSDKError

async def attempt(label, **limits):
    opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(model=MODEL, allowed_tools=["Read", "Bash", "Edit"], **limits)
    try:
        async for m in query(prompt="Find the failing test and fix it", options=opts):
            if isinstance(m, ResultMessage):
                print(f"{label}: subtype={m.subtype} turns={m.num_turns} cost=${m.total_cost_usd}")
    except ClaudeSDKError as e:           # single-shot query() raises AFTER yielding the error ResultMessage
        print(f"{label}: raised -> {e}")

async def main():
    await attempt("turn cap", max_turns=1)
    await attempt("budget cap", max_budget_usd=0.003)
    await attempt("no caps")

asyncio.run(main())

Output (captured from a real run against the offline mock SDK):

turn cap: subtype=error_max_turns turns=1 cost=$0.0063
turn cap: raised -> Reached maximum number of turns
budget cap: subtype=error_max_budget_usd turns=1 cost=$0.0063
budget cap: raised -> Reached maximum budget
no caps: subtype=success turns=3 cost=$0.0084

Reading the output

  • turn cap: subtype=error_max_turns: max_turns=1 stopped the run: the result message says why.
  • raised ->: Single-shot query() then raises; wrap it in try/except.
  • budget cap: max_budget_usd stopped the spend with its own subtype.
  • no caps: subtype=success: Unconstrained, the same task finishes in 3 turns.
  • Retries: retry transient failures with backoff at your layer; make tools idempotent; resume the session instead of restarting from scratch.
  • Cost: total_cost_usd is a client-side estimate; usage covers the main loop, model_usage includes subagents. Use cheaper models for subagents, cap with max_turns/max_budget_usd.
  • Observability: hooks (Pre/PostToolUse) emit structured logs; capture session ids, turns, cost, denied permissions (permission_denials).
  • Testing: mock tool handlers, assert on hook decisions, run evals on fixed prompts, use plan mode or read-only tools in CI.
  • Deployment: container per run/session, secrets from a vault, persistent session store for resumption, queue long jobs, never bypassPermissions outside a sandbox.

1. Enterprise document research agent

Business problem

Staff waste hours finding and summarizing scattered internal documents.

Proposed solution

A read-mostly agent finds files, reads them and writes one summary file.

Components involved

Glob, Grep, Read, Write; acceptEdits mode; system prompt requiring citations.

Execution flow

  1. Glob lists docs
  2. Read VPN and MFA docs
  3. Write summary.md (auto-approved edit)
  4. Return confirmation

Relevant Agent SDK concepts

Built-in tools, permission_mode=acceptEdits, max_turns, system prompt.

5. Human-approved execution agent

Business problem

Refunds are automatable, but large ones need a manager.

Proposed solution

A custom refund tool plus a can_use_tool policy: auto-approve small amounts, require human approval above a threshold, log everything.

Components involved

@tool, create_sdk_mcp_server, can_use_tool, audit log.

Execution flow

  1. Claude requests refund $40: auto-approved
  2. Claude requests refund $250: callback denies/queues
  3. Claude reports the outcome
  4. Audit log lists both decisions

Relevant Agent SDK concepts

Permission callbacks, human-in-the-loop, custom tools.

Architecture diagram

Python implementation and real output

import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

# Scenario 5 - Human-approved execution agent (refunds)
from claude_agent_sdk import (tool, create_sdk_mcp_server, ClaudeSDKClient, ClaudeAgentOptions,
                              PermissionResultAllow, PermissionResultDeny)
from show import show

@tool("issue_refund", "Refund an order", {"order": str, "amount": float})
async def issue_refund(args):
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": f"refunded ${args['amount']:.2f} on {args['order']}"}]}

payments = create_sdk_mcp_server("payments", tools=[issue_refund])
AUDIT = []                                           # who/what/decision

async def can_use_tool(name, tool_input, ctx):
    amount = tool_input.get("amount", 0)
    if name.endswith("issue_refund") and amount > 100:           # policy: large refunds need a human
        decision = "denied"                                      # stand-in for a real approval UI
        AUDIT.append((name, tool_input, decision))
        return PermissionResultDeny(message=f"Refund of ${amount} needs manager approval; request queued")
    AUDIT.append((name, tool_input, "auto-approved"))
    return PermissionResultAllow()

opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(model=MODEL, mcp_servers={"payments": payments}, can_use_tool=can_use_tool)

async def main():
    async with ClaudeSDKClient(options=opts) as c:
        await c.query("Refund order O-1 ($40) and order O-2 ($250)")
        async for m in c.receive_response():
            show(m)
    print("--- audit log ---")
    for row in AUDIT: print(row)

asyncio.run(main())

Callback (dynamic, per-call) rather than permission mode (too coarse).

6. Enterprise knowledge assistant

Business problem

Employees ask HR/IT questions answered across many documents.

Proposed solution

A custom search tool locates the source, Read fetches it, and a hook logs usage.

Components involved

Custom SDK MCP tool, Read, PostToolUse hook, grounding system prompt.

Execution flow

  1. search_kb finds docs/vpn.md
  2. Read opens it
  3. Answer with citation
  4. Hook records tools used

Relevant Agent SDK concepts

Custom tools, hooks for observability, system prompt grounding.

Architecture diagram

Python implementation and real output

import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

# Scenario 6 - Enterprise knowledge assistant (custom search tool + hook logging)
from claude_agent_sdk import tool, create_sdk_mcp_server, query, ClaudeAgentOptions, HookMatcher
from show import show

@tool("search_kb", "Search the internal knowledge base; returns matching document paths", {"query": str})
async def search_kb(args):
    hits = {"vpn": "docs/vpn.md", "mfa": "docs/mfa.md"}
    return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": hits.get(args["query"].lower(), "no match")}]}

kb = create_sdk_mcp_server("kb", tools=[search_kb])
LOG = []
async def log_tool(input_data, tool_use_id, context):
    LOG.append(input_data["tool_name"]); return {}

opts = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    model=MODEL,
    system_prompt="Answer employee questions only from the knowledge base. Cite the source path.",
    mcp_servers={"kb": kb},
    allowed_tools=["mcp__kb__search_kb", "Read"],
    hooks={"PostToolUse": [HookMatcher(hooks=[log_tool])]},
)
async def main():
    async for m in query(prompt="How do I get VPN access?", options=opts):

import os, asyncio
os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"] = "sk-ant-mock-0000000000"   # MOCK key (real runs: your own key)
MODEL = "claude-sonnet-5-5"                                    # model id used by the agent loop

from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions, AssistantMessage, TextBlock, ToolUseBlock, ResultMessage

async def main():
    options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
        model=MODEL,
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Glob", "Grep"],   # pre-approved, read-only built-in tools
        max_turns=8,                              # safety cap on agent-loop iterations
        cwd="./contracts",                        # working directory for the tools
    )
    # query() returns an async iterator: nothing runs until we iterate
    async for msg in query(prompt="List every contract that renews in 2026.", options=options):
        if isinstance(msg, AssistantMessage):
            for block in msg.content:
                if isinstance(block, ToolUseBlock): print("[tool]", block.name, block.input)   # Claude chose a tool
                elif isinstance(block, TextBlock): print(block.text)                           # Claude's text
        elif isinstance(msg, ResultMessage):          # always the last message
            print(f"turns={msg.num_turns} cost=${msg.total_cost_usd} session={msg.session_id}")

asyncio.run(main())

cheat.summary: Designing agent systems on the Claude Agent SDK: the agent loop, query() vs ClaudeSDKClient, built-in and custom tools, MCP, subagents, deterministic hooks, sessions, permissions and enterprise hardening.

domains.title: 1. Agent SDK Fundamentals & Configuration
points: What the SDK gives you: the agent loop (reason → act → observe), built-in tools, permissions, hooks, MCP wiring and session handling. With the plain Messages API you build all of that yourself.
query() vs ClaudeSDKClient: query() is a single exchange returning an async iterator; ClaudeSDKClient keeps a session for multi-turn chat and supports interrupt().

Message stream: SystemMessage → AssistantMessage(s) → ResultMessage. The ResultMessage carries subtype, turns, cost and session_id; max_turns caps loop iterations (exceeding it yields error_max_turns).
System prompts: a custom string replaces the default; the claude_code preset with append keeps the tool-use guidance and adds yours — prefer the preset for tool-heavy agents.

domains.title: 2. Tools, Custom Tools & MCP
points: Built-in tool risk ladder: Read/Glob/Grep are low risk; Bash runs arbitrary commands and is the highest risk — scope or deny it explicitly.
allowed_tools pre-approves; it does not remove. Other tools still exist and prompt for permission. Use disallowed_tools to block.
Custom tools: clear JSON schema, precise description of when to call, explicit error handling; return is_error: true so Claude can recover inside the loop.
MCP servers connect external systems through a standard protocol; tool names are namespaced (mcp__server__tool) and MCP tools obey the same permission model.

domains.title: 3. Subagents, Hooks & Sessions
points: Subagents isolate context: a research or log-analysis subagent burns its own tokens and returns only a synthesis to the parent — the fix when verbose tool output pollutes the orchestrator.
Hooks are deterministic: PreToolUse hooks intercept tool calls before execution and can block or require approval — unlike prompt instructions, which are probabilistic.

Sessions: every run has a session_id; resume to continue with full context. Permission modes: default, acceptEdits (auto-approves file edits in the working directory), plan, bypassPermissions (sandbox only).

domains.title: 4. Security, Errors & Enterprise Patterns
points: Least privilege first: narrow allowed_tools, explicit deny rules for destructive commands, approvals on irreversible actions, human-in-the-loop before high-impact writes.
Error subtypes matter: distinguish error_max_turns (raise the cap or decompose) from tool failures (fix the tool or its inputs) from permission denials (adjust scope deliberately).
Production shape: deterministic workflow for the standard path, agent invoked at the genuinely open-ended decision points; log turns, cost and session ids per run.

code.title: query() with scoped tools, max_turns and the ResultMessage
code.description: The canonical single-exchange agent run: pre-approved tools, a turn cap, and reading cost/turns off the final ResultMessage.
code.code:
import asyncio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    allowed_tools=["Read", "Glob", "Grep"],   # pre-approved; others still prompt
    disallowed_tools=["Bash"],                 # removed outright
    max_turns=8,                                # safety cap -> error_max_turns beyond
    system_prompt={"type": "preset", "preset": "claude_code",
                   "append": "Only summarize; never modify files."},
)

async def main():
    async for msg in query(prompt="Summarize the contracts in ./docs", options=options):
        kind = type(msg).__name__
        if kind == "ResultMessage":
            print("subtype:", msg.subtype)        # 'success' | 'error_max_turns' | ...
            print("turns:", msg.num_turns, "cost: $", msg.total_cost_usd)
            print("session:", msg.session_id)     # persist to resume later

asyncio.run(main())
